unit.title: This season, live
unit.summary: Weekly templates driven by live data: previews, recaps, title picture, driver and team form.

lessons.title: This weekend: what to watch
lessons.objective: Read a race preview: circuit type, tyre picks and what matters most.

payload.prompt: Is this circuit a street circuit, high-speed track, or balanced layout?

options.text: Street circuit
options.explanation: Tight, bumpy, walls close. Track position and tyre life matter most.

options.text: High-speed track
options.explanation: Fast corners, long straights. Downforce and aero efficiency rule.

options.text: Balanced
options.explanation: Mix of corners and straights. No single style dominates.

explanation.correct: Right. Street circuits like Monaco and Singapore are tight and unforgiving.
explanation.incorrect: Circuit type shapes strategy: street circuits favor track position, high-speed layouts favor outright pace.
explanation.sayThisLine: Street circuits are all about staying ahead.

payload.prompt: Three compounds are hard (white), medium (yellow), soft (red). Hot weather favors which?

options.text: Hard for durability
options.explanation: Hards last longer but are slower per lap.

options.text: Soft for speed
options.explanation: Softs are fastest but wear quicker, especially in heat.

options.text: Medium as a middle ground
options.explanation: Medium is balanced but not the answer in hot weather.

explanation.correct: Right. Heat stresses tyres. Softs wear fastest but deliver the pace teams need when track temps rise.
explanation.incorrect: Hot tracks favor softer compounds for grip, though the trade-off is short tyre life.

payload.prompt: Is a sprint weekend longer or shorter in total running time than a regular weekend?

scene.alt: Saturday has SQ1-SQ3 then a 100km sprint race. Sunday has regular qualifying and the Grand Prix.

explanation.correct: Right. Sprints add a Saturday race, so total track time grows despite one fewer Friday practice.
explanation.incorrect: Sprints add an extra Saturday race, so even with one fewer Friday session, the total running time is more.

payload.prompt: Track improves lap by lap on Friday. Set up for Friday pace or Sunday race conditions?

situation.narrative: The track is cool and slippery on Friday morning but will be 15°C hotter and quicker on Sunday.

options.label: Tune for Friday: get the most from today
options.consequence: You dial in the car for cool, low-grip conditions. Sunday comes and the setup is too extreme: understeer or oversteer in the heat.
considerations: Friday practice is for learning, not dialling in the race setup.
Track evolution means a Friday setup is already half-obsolete by qualifying.

options.label: Target Sunday: prepare for the race
options.consequence: You build a setup that will work Sunday and Saturday qualifying. Friday times are slower but meaningful.
considerations: Sunday is the race. That is what counts for points.
A setup that works in heat and grip is a setup that works in the race.

options.label: Chase Saturday: split the difference
options.consequence: You aim for qualifying conditions. Friday times are rough, Sunday requires tweaks.
considerations: Targeting qualifying can work if you do not over-commit.

payload.expertNote: Race teams dial for race day, using Friday to understand the car's sensitivity.
payload.sayThisLine: Friday data points to Sunday pace.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: They are worried about the new kerbs this weekend. No Friday data yet.

payload.question: Why is she concerned?

options.text: New kerbs mean the car set-up could be wrong
options.explanation: Unfamiliar kerbs change how the car feels and setup balance.

options.text: Kerbs are less safe
options.explanation: Safety concerns are not mentioned in this context.

options.text: The team will not have spare parts
options.explanation: Spare parts inventory is unrelated to circuit kerbs.

payload.translation: New track features mean the car's behaviour is unpredictable until Friday running. Less time to dial it in.

followUps.why: Shows you understand that practice data builds confidence.

lessons.title: Last race in plain English
lessons.objective: Decode last race's result, strategy calls and controversies.

payload.prompt: A driver pits on lap 20 while the leader is on lap 21. The undercut works if...?

options.text: Fresh tyres help the undercut car lap faster than the leader does before stopping.
options.explanation: Yes, speed on fresh rubber is the whole point.

options.text: The pit stop takes less than two seconds.
options.explanation: A fast stop helps but the key is the pace gain afterward.

options.text: Both cars pit on the same lap.
options.explanation: If they pit together, there is no undercut.

explanation.correct: Right. The undercut works because new tyres are quicker. If the undertaker laps faster than the leader does on old tyres, the undertaker jumps ahead when the leader finally stops.
explanation.incorrect: An undercut needs the undertaker to be quicker on fresh tyres than the leader on old ones, closing the gap and then some.

payload.prompt: Car stops under safety car (12 seconds pit loss). Was this good luck or bad luck for the car?

scene.alt: A car pits during a safety-car period when all cars are bunched and running slow.

explanation.correct: Right. A 12-second stop under the safety car is cheap. Normal pit loss is about 20 seconds, so the safety car cut the cost in half.
explanation.incorrect: Under the safety car, the pit loss is roughly halved because the field is bunched. A 12-second stop is a lucky timing.

payload.prompt: A driver finishes second and gets a five-second time penalty. What happens to their result?

options.text: They stay second; penalty points are added to their licence.
options.explanation: Penalty points and time penalties are separate things.

options.text: Five seconds are added to their race time, potentially dropping their place.
options.explanation: Right; a five-second penalty can change the final order.

options.text: They are disqualified from this race.
options.explanation: That would be a harsher penalty like a black flag.

explanation.correct: Right. A time penalty is added to the race time; it can swing the finishing order if the margin is tight.
explanation.incorrect: A time penalty adds seconds to the final race time, not licence points. Five seconds can drop a driver from second to fourth if others are close.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: He was leading by ten seconds and then DNF. The car was the fastest out there.

payload.question: What is she saying?

options.text: He retired from the lead due to a failure, despite clear pace
options.explanation: DNF is Did Not Finish; he quit the race while leading.

options.text: He finished first but lost the title
options.explanation: DNF means he did not finish at all.

options.text: The car was damaged but he kept racing
options.explanation: Damaged or not, DNF means he stopped.

payload.translation: He had to retire (mechanical failure or crash) from a commanding lead. A wasted day because finish position and points matter, not pace.

followUps.why: Shows curiosity about the underlying cause.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: The pit wall gambled on the undercut and it paid off this time.

payload.question: What did the strategist do?

options.text: Pitted earlier than the rival to jump ahead on fresh tyres
options.explanation: That is the definition of an undercut strategy.

options.text: Stayed out longer while the rival pitted to gain clear air
options.explanation: That is an overcut, not an undercut.

options.text: Took a risk and it did not work
options.explanation: She said it 'paid off', meaning it succeeded.

payload.translation: The team called an earlier stop, hoping the fresh tyres would let the driver lap faster than the rival and jump track position.

followUps.line: Did the other team see it coming?

lessons.title: The championship picture
lessons.objective: Read standings and work out who can still win and what they need.

payload.prompt: Leader has 175 points with four races left. Each race awards a max of 25 points. Can anyone catch them?

options.text: No; 175 is unbeatable
options.explanation: 175 plus three more wins = 250. Rivals could still catch up.

options.text: Yes; if a rival wins all four races and the leader scores zero
options.explanation: Possible, though unlikely. Math: 175 + 0 vs rival on, say, 155 + 100.

options.text: Only if there is a red flag or crash
options.explanation: Not true. Raw pace and strategy decide it.

explanation.correct: Right. With four races and 25 points per win, a 20-point deficit can be closed. Math matters in the title race.
explanation.incorrect: A 20-point lead with four races left is not safe if rivals are faster or lucky.

payload.prompt: Three drivers are within 30 points with six races left. How many different final outcomes are mathematically possible?

explanation.correct: Right. With six races and tight gaps, all three can still win depending on results. Realistic: three drivers all have a path.
explanation.incorrect: Six races, three contenders within 30 points: mathematically all three can clinch or be eliminated depending on outcomes.

payload.prompt: In the constructors' championship, two drivers from the same team score. Does that make it easier or harder to win?

scene.alt: A team with two drivers both finishing in the points, so both sets of points count.

explanation.correct: Right. Two drivers scoring double the points is a big advantage over a rival with one car scoring.
explanation.incorrect: Two drivers scoring points is better than one. That is why team depth matters in the constructors' championship.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: If he wins the next three and the leader finishes fifth, it is suddenly a fight.

payload.question: What is she calculating?

options.text: The gap could narrow dramatically if pace flips
options.explanation: Three wins plus the leader's bad result is a swing.

options.text: Points are awarded only for wins
options.explanation: Points are awarded down to tenth.

options.text: The leader will definitely lose the title
options.explanation: Three races change the gap, but not destiny.

payload.translation: A few races of swapped fortune—one driver winning, the other scoring little—can flip a seemingly locked title.

followUps.line: How many points is that swing?
followUps.why: Tests understanding of the point scale.

lessons.title: {{driver}} this season
lessons.objective: Explain how {{driver}} is performing this season and why.

payload.prompt: A driver qualifies 0.5 seconds slower than their teammate but wins the race. What does that tell you?

options.text: Race pace matters more than qualifying
options.explanation: Sunday matters, and race pace can trump one-lap pace.

options.text: The car is unbalanced for qualifying
options.explanation: Possible, but the driver's race pace strength is the takeaway.

options.text: The teammate made a mistake
options.explanation: Maybe, but the winner still had to execute.

explanation.correct: Right. Qualifying pace and race pace are separate. Some drivers shine over one lap, others over a distance.
explanation.incorrect: Race wins come from race pace. A driver quicker on Sunday than Saturday is the whole profile.

payload.prompt: Is a 0.1 second qualifying gap to a teammate big or small?

scene.alt: Qualifying session where one driver posts a 1:35.2 and the teammate laps a 1:35.3.

explanation.correct: Right. Tenths are huge in qualifying. One-tenth from the same car and driver in the same heat is a real performance gap.
explanation.incorrect: In qualifying, a tenth of a second is a sizable gap. Over a season, it compounds into title relevance.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: He is quicker on Sunday. Qualifying is not where we win.

payload.question: What is she saying about {{driver}}'s strengths?

options.text: {{driver}} is stronger in races than over one lap
options.explanation: Sunday pace trumps Saturday pace for her driver.

options.text: {{driver}} only scores points on race day
options.explanation: Qualifying place sets the race start.

options.text: {{driver}}'s teammate is faster
options.explanation: Not necessarily; Sunday pace is a strength, not a weakness.

payload.translation: {{driver}} may not set the grid on fire in one-lap runs, but over a race distance they find pace.

followUps.line: Does that mean qualifying does not matter?
followUps.why: Explores the interplay of grid position and race pace.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: Two DNFs cost him the title this season. The car speed is there, reliability is not.

payload.question: What is her point?

options.text: {{driver}}'s teammate is faster
options.explanation: Reliability is about finishes, not speed comparison.

options.text: {{driver}} has the pace but car failures hurt points
options.explanation: A DNF scores zero no matter how fast you were.

options.text: {{driver}} is not good at defending
options.explanation: Unrelated to mechanical failure.

payload.translation: {{driver}} is quick but mechanical issues are costing points that would change the title race.

followUps.line: Is the team fixing the reliability issues?
followUps.why: Shows you understand that speed and car fitness are separate.

lessons.title: {{team}} this season
lessons.objective: Explain {{team}}'s form and what to watch in their race.

payload.prompt: {{team}} is third in constructors with 140 points, 30 behind second. With eight races left, are they still in it?

options.text: No; 30 points is too big to close
options.explanation: Eight races, max 25 per race: 30 is within reach if {{team}} finds pace.

options.text: Yes; if {{team}} outscores second-place consistently
options.explanation: Possible, though it requires a sustained turnaround.

options.text: Maybe, but it depends on reliability
options.explanation: Both pace and finishing are crucial.

explanation.correct: Right. {{team}} needs to be quicker and consistent. Eight races, 30-point gap, is tight but alive.
explanation.incorrect: {{team}} is in it if they can outscore their rivals over the final races.

payload.prompt: {{team}}'s power unit is on the grid in 2026. Is this a boost or a challenge?

scene.alt: A team's engine supplier status for the new regulation era.

explanation.correct: Right. A regulation reset scrambles the grid. New power unit rules mean all engine makers start from scratch.
explanation.incorrect: A new regulation era is a reset. {{team}}'s success in 2026 depends on who built the better power unit, not 2025 form.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: {{team}} brought a big upgrade this month and the pace jumped two tenths.

payload.question: What upgrade probably helped?

options.text: A new wing or floor part, improving aero efficiency
options.explanation: Mid-season upgrades are usually aero gains.

options.text: A new engine that violates regulations
options.explanation: Engine rules are strict; major changes are rare mid-season.

options.text: A rule change that favored {{team}}
options.explanation: Rules change for all teams equally.

payload.translation: {{team}} deployed a new aerodynamic part that gave them a step forward in pace.

followUps.line: Will it get copied by other teams?
followUps.why: Shows you understand F1's equipment evolution.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: We are second in the constructors but we keep losing cars to failures. If we finish every race, we are first.

payload.question: What is she telling you?

options.text: {{team}} has the pace but car reliability is costing points
options.explanation: Pace and finishing are both necessary.

options.text: {{team}} should blame the engine supplier
options.explanation: Reliability is a team responsibility.

options.text: {{team}} is guaranteed to win the title
options.explanation: 'If we finish every race' is a condition, not a guarantee.

payload.translation: {{team}} is fast, but mechanical issues are robbing them of points they would otherwise score.

followUps.why: Shows you are following the season's storylines.

lessons.title: The 2026 rules, still in motion
lessons.objective: Follow mid-season tweaks to the regulations and why teams argue about them.

payload.prompt: The FIA issues a technical directive in June clarifying the flexi-wing rules. Is this normal?

options.text: Yes; mid-season directives close loopholes teams find
options.explanation: Correct. Teams exploit ambiguities; the FIA clarifies.

options.text: No; rules are locked from the start of the season
options.explanation: Regulations can be tweaked if a loophole is found.

options.text: Only if the FIA made an error in the rulebook
options.explanation: Directives come for loopholes, not just errors.

explanation.correct: Right. Technical directives are the FIA's way of closing ambiguities mid-season.
explanation.incorrect: Teams push the edges of the rulebook. Directives close the gaps and reset competition.

payload.prompt: ADUO lets underperforming engine makers take extra upgrades mid-season. Is that fair?

scene.alt: A manufacturer that is off the pace gets extra development chances.

explanation.correct: Right. ADUO is a safety net to keep engine suppliers competitive. Without it, one weak supplier could dominate.
explanation.incorrect: ADUO is a balance mechanism. If one engine supplier falls too far behind, the cost makes racing less compelling for fans.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: The FIA ruled on compression ratios yesterday. Honda and Ferrari do not agree.

payload.question: What is the dispute about?

options.text: How tightly the engine squeezes the fuel-air mix, and how it is measured
options.explanation: Compression ratio is a spec limit; measuring it is where disagreement arises.

options.text: Who gets more fuel for races
options.explanation: Fuel is a different regulation.

options.text: Which team is allowed to upgrade their engine
options.explanation: Upgrades are managed separately.

payload.translation: Engine makers dispute whether the rulebook's compression-ratio measurement is fair, especially if one method favors someone's design.

followUps.line: Does this affect the race on Sunday?

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: The FIA tightened the rules on active-aero deployment. Now you cannot open the wings in braking.

payload.question: Why would the FIA do that?

options.text: To prevent dangerous loss of grip during braking
options.explanation: Safety is a core reason for wing regulations.

options.text: To slow down one team
options.explanation: Rules are applied equally.

options.text: Fans complained it looked weird
options.explanation: Aesthetics do not drive safety regulations.

payload.translation: The FIA refined active-aero rules to prevent risky wing movements at high braking loads.

followUps.line: Did the ruling help or hurt specific teams?
followUps.why: Shows you understand that regulations have winners and losers.

lessons.title: Silly season: who is moving
lessons.objective: Follow driver-market stories and upcoming seat changes.

payload.prompt: Silly season peaks in which part of the season?

options.text: Early season, before the title is decided
options.explanation: Early news does happen, but it is quieter.

options.text: Mid-season, when the title picture clarifies
options.explanation: Right. Teams know who is quick and who is free to move.

options.text: After the season ends
options.explanation: Announcements come, but the buzz is mid-season.

explanation.correct: Right. Once teams know their competitive position, they plan for next year. Speculation and signings peak mid-season.
explanation.incorrect: Silly season is loudest mid-season when teams know their form and start plotting signings.

payload.prompt: Does a junior-programme seat or a reserve-driver role carry more opportunity to race?

scene.alt: Career options for a young driver: academy funding or pit lane standby.

explanation.correct: Right. A junior programme (like Red Bull's) funds F2 and F3 teams. A reserve waits in the paddock for an injury or disqualification.
explanation.incorrect: A junior programme offers funded racing every weekend. A reserve might never race if both drivers stay healthy.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: A young driver won F2 this year. Is there a seat for him in 2026?

payload.question: What determines if he gets an F1 drive?

options.text: F2 title, super-licence points, and available seats
options.explanation: Merit, licensing and timing all matter.

options.text: Just the F2 championship
options.explanation: Many F2 winners wait for a seat.

options.text: Whether a team likes his name
options.explanation: Driving record and licensing are objective.

payload.translation: F2 success earns super-licence points, but empty F1 seats are the real gating factor. Great juniors sometimes wait years.

followUps.line: Which teams have open seats next year?
followUps.why: Shows you are tracking the silly-season movement.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: Everyone is talking about his contract. Does he stay or chase the big seat?

payload.question: What is she asking about?

options.text: Whether the driver extends at his team or moves to a stronger one
options.explanation: Staying vs. chasing is the age-old choice.

options.text: Whether he can afford a new contract
options.explanation: Teams offer contracts; drivers do not usually pay them.

options.text: Whether he will be team principal someday
options.explanation: Unrelated to the current seat.

payload.translation: A talented driver at a mid-grid team is weighing loyalty or a move to a championship-contending team.

followUps.why: Invites her perspective; opinion-based follow-ups are better than just facts.

lessons.title: Circuit primer: {{region}} and the next race
lessons.objective: Prepare for the next race: layout, circuit personality and likely strategy.

payload.prompt: {{region}} is known for {{circuitType}}. How does that shape strategy?

options.text: Street layout: track position and tyres matter most
options.explanation: Tight circuits favour being ahead and managing degradation.

options.text: High-speed: pace and aero efficiency win
options.explanation: Wings and power matter where grip is high.

options.text: It does not matter; strategy is the same everywhere
options.explanation: Circuit type shapes everything.

explanation.correct: Right. Each circuit type demands different trade-offs.
explanation.incorrect: Track layout shapes pit strategy, tyre choice and setup philosophy.

payload.prompt: Where is {{region}}'s pit lane located on the circuit?

image.alt: Map of {{region}} circuit showing pit lane and main features.

hotspots.label: Pit lane
hotspots.feedback: Right. The pit lane is where teams service their cars during the race.

hotspots.label: Starting grid
hotspots.feedback: That is the starting grid, not the pit lane.

payload.prompt: Identify the main passing opportunity at {{region}}. Tap the braking zone.

image.alt: {{region}} circuit layout showing high-speed and slow corners.

hotspots.label: Turn 1 braking zone
hotspots.feedback: Right. The braking zone into Turn 1 is where most passing happens.

hotspots.label: High-speed sweeper
hotspots.feedback: High-speed corners are hard to pass; the braking zone is better.

payload.prompt: Is a one-stop strategy likely to work at {{region}} given its length and pace?

scene.alt: Circuit with moderate pace and tyre-wearing characteristics.

explanation.correct: Right. {{region}} allows one-stop strategies if tyre management is good.
explanation.incorrect: Track length and wear rates favour one stop if the driver and team execute well.

payload.prompt: Friday practice shows tyres degrade slowly at {{region}}. Do you plan one stop or two?

situation.narrative: Friday data suggests tyres can run 40-45 laps without hitting the cliff. The race is 60 laps.

options.label: Plan for one stop: tyres last, pit once late
options.consequence: If tyres degrade faster in the race heat, you hit the cliff before lap 60. A forced second stop drops you.
considerations: Friday is cool. Race day is hotter and speeds are faster, stressing tyres more.

options.label: Plan for two stops: pit early, maintain pace
options.consequence: Two stops cost time, but fresh tyres keep you competitive. You control the race.
considerations: Two stops are safe. If tyres last longer, you can adjust on Sunday.
Staying on pace matters in a tight field.

options.label: Decide Sunday morning based on Saturday data
options.consequence: You gather more info, but qualifying set-up and Saturday running constrain your options.
considerations: Flexibility is good, but Friday prep informs Sunday race planning.

payload.expertNote: Friday data is a guide, not gospel. Hot-weather degradation is real.
payload.sayThisLine: Friday cool, Sunday hot. Plan for heat.
